quote.translation: Rather, all these chances themselves, τὰ εἰκῇ φερόμενα (what is brought about at random), are embraced by one deeply hidden necessity, εἱμαρ- μένη (fate), and chance itself is a mere instrument of that necessity" (Schopenhauer, Sämtliche Werke hrsg. v. Deussen, IV. S. 228).

quote.translation: "At the root of this mundus phaenomenon (world of appearances), ruled by chance, there will lie, wholly and everywhere, a mundus intelligibilis (intelligible world) that governs chance itself" (Ib., 232).

quote.translation: The concept of fate is "the deep-lying root-unity of necessity and contingency" (Ib., 235), "the final unity of necessity and contingency" (Ib.).

regions.text: 『必然性と偶然性との深く横はつた根の統一』（1,235）『必然性と偶然性との最後の統一』（）が運命の概念である。「だまだま行信を獲ば遠く御漱をようこべ』（飲行信故呼といふ育葉にも同じ意が表はれてるる。かの六師の宿命論と無因論とも差別し難い一致點を有つてゐる。「一切皆因宿命造』といふのと「一切皆無因無緣』といふのとは結局は同じことであ、る（中阿合経怒三、度趣）。

quote.translation: The same sense finds expression in the words "If by chance you obtain practice and faith, rejoice far back in the conditions of past lives" (Kyōgyōshinshō, Preface), and the fatalism and the acausalism of the six teachers likewise share a point of agreement that is hard to tell apart, since to say "all is made by former destiny" and to say "all is without cause and without condition" come in the end to the same thing (Madhyama Āgama, fascicle 3, Du jing).

regions.text: 偶然と運命との間にかやうな内的關係が存するごとに基いて、ヰルヘルムフォンシ"ルツもその考偶然に「運命の前形式」（EineVorformdesSchicksals）といふ別名を與へてある。

quote.translation: It is because such an inner relation holds between chance and fate that Wilhelm von Scholz gives his book Chance the alternative title A Preliminary Form of Fate (Eine Vorform des Schicksals).

regions.text: 園木田獨歩も運命論者」の中で甲が「僕は運命論者ではありません』と云つたに對してこをして「それでは偶然論者ですか』と詰間させてゐる。この結間は單なる皮肉に過ぎぬもので、運命と個然とが果意同一のものであることが前提されてるる。

quote.translation: In Kunikida Doppo's "The Fatalist", when A says "I am not a fatalist", B is made to press him with "Then are you a believer in chance?", and this retort, which is no more than irony, presupposes that fate and chance are ultimately one and the same.

In Mushanokōji Saneatsu's "The Man Who Plays Go with Fate" we find the words "Fate is something of which one cannot tell where it is lying in wait", and here one might just as well say "chance" in place of "fate".
